results.content: What are the different ways that a function can be represented? A function is a mapping from inputs to outputs; it can be represented in multiple equivalent ways depending on context, purpose, and the audience. - Cons: not all functions have simple closed forms A function is a mapping from inputs to outputs; it can be represented in multiple equivalent ways depending on context, purpose, and the audience. - Cons: not all functions have simple closed forms (e.g., fractal or piecewise definitions). - Use when: defining functions by computation, iterative processes, or when closed form is unknown. - Pros: concrete for computation; can represent arbitrary computable functions. - Cons: imprecise for exact values; high-dimensional functions are harder to visualize. 6. Set-theoretic Definition (graph of the function) - Description: Function defined as a set of ordered pairs {(x, f(x)) | x in domain}, or as a subset of Cartesian product with functional property. - Use when: functions with qualitatively different behavior across regions (absolute value, step functions). - Description: Function defined by an equation relating x and y, e.g., F(x,y)=0; y is a (possibly multi-valued) function of x implicitly. - Cons: requires implicit function theorem conditions for local explicit representation; may be multi-valued. Transform / Operator Domain (e.g., Laplace, Fourier, Z-transform) - Description: Representing a function via its transform: F(s)=∫ e^{−st} f(t) dt, or frequency spectrum. Functional / Mapping between function spaces - Description: A function whose inputs and/or outputs are themselves functions (e.g., linear functional, operator). - Use when: functional analysis, calculus of variations, differential operators. Implicitly via Properties or Axioms - Description: Characterized by properties rather than explicit form (e.g., “the unique continuous function f on [0,1] with f(0)=0 and f′(x)=g(x)”). - Use when: machine learning, complexity theory, or when functions are learned/approximated from data. - Use when: solving PDEs with singular sources or in generalized-function theory. 2. results.content: Stack Exchange network consists of 183 Q&A communities including Stack Overflow, the largest, most trusted online community for developers to learn, share their knowledge, and build their careers. # Extending a function beyond the completion/closure of its domain. In analysis there are certain theorems that tell under which conditions you can continuously extend a continuous functions to the closure/completion of its domain (which actually give the same set, since when talking about completions we have to be (at least) in a metric space). * Every uniformly continuous mapping between a metric space and a complete metric can be extended uniformly continuous to a mapping between the completion of the domain and the range. * Every continuous function on a dense subset can be continuously extend to the closure of that subspace (which is by definition of "dense", the whole space). What I'm looking for is a collection of theorems that tell me under which circumstances one can extend a continuous function *beyond* the completion or the closure of it's domain. The only theorem of this kind that I know of is the famous Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem (which applies to function whose domain is already a closed set). $\begingroup$ For linear functionals the Hahn-Banach theorem provides conditions under which functions defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space (/wiki/Hahn%E2%80%93Banach\_theorem). 1. unique extension from a non-closed set to its closure.
